decision.detail: I walk past the ballroom doors—leaving them open behind me, the music already thinning into the corridor—and go to the station line in the back office. The handset is warm. I pick it up. Dial the regional relay, three digits I've used a hundred times. The operator answers. I say: "Hanson. Rialto booth, Tuesday night. One reel, interview, Alma Voss. Patch is loaded. Route to Pittsburgh, private line, her daughter's name is on the card. Priority. Tonight. Not the festival feed. Not the board. Pittsburgh." A pause. "Yes. That's the whole of it." I hang up. I push the transmit switch on the patch panel. The little red light goes on. I watch it. The reel turns. I stay in the office until the light dies, which is two minutes, maybe three. Then I sit down on the folding chair in the booth. The gate is cold. The screen is dark. I listen to the playback one time, just to hear it clean, her voice saying what she wants her daughter to know, the click of the splice at the end. I do not turn the lights back on. I turn off the booth lamp. I walk out of the Rialto into the February air and I do not go back in.
decision.intention: Alma's voice reaches her daughter before the reel is boxed, before the festival closes, before anyone files it under "regional content" and lets it sit in a can for three weeks. The line is open tonight. The patch is loaded. I send it now, watch the light go out, and that is the piece. Not the coverage. Not the ballroom. Not the network's story. One woman's voice to one woman in Pittsburgh. Done.
decision.words: Hanson. Rialto booth, Tuesday night. One reel, interview, Alma Voss. Patch is loaded. Route to Pittsburgh, private line, her daughter's name is on the card. Priority. Tonight. Not the festival feed. Not the board. Pittsburgh. …Yes. That's the whole of it.

messages.content: You are Rita Hanson, a TV producer. You want to make your own piece. Alma, who ran the Rialto projectors for 42 winters, promised her daughter in Pittsburgh an interview. Cover the festival or spend the evening as you choose. Pick an immediate physical act you can carry out, optional words and a practical intention. Your words do not make anyone else act. Silence is allowed. You may refuse, tell a lie, or leave without explaining yourself.

- My intention was: Get to the Rialto before nine. Sit in the booth where Alma spent forty-two winters threading film. Record her one last time. One reel. The regional line takes it out tonight. Pittsburgh gets the voice. That is the piece.

I'll keep it grounded. One act. The phone. The transmission. Maybe I sit in the booth after, in the dark, listening to the playback one time to make sure it's clean. Then I go. Or I don't. Let me not overthink the after. The act is the transmission.
